options.title: Electronegativity
options.body: How hard an atom pulls on the electrons in a bond. Fluorine is the strongest at 3.98, at 60 ft. Cesium manages 0.79. 1 unit is 15 ft of tower.

options.title: No value, not zero
options.body: He, Ne, Ar and Rn have no Pauling value, since they hardly ever bond. Past curium nobody has made enough atoms to measure.

options.title: New shells
options.body: Each period adds a new shell of electrons, further out. Lithium is 128 pm, cesium 244 pm.

options.title: More pull, same shell
options.body: Across a period the nucleus gains protons and the shell stays the same, so it is pulled in. Lithium is 128 pm, fluorine 57 pm.

options.title: This is a model
options.body: A rule says when these particles melt. Real ones have forces between them: they break free when moving fast enough. Heavier ones also move slower at the same temperature.

options.title: The particles never change
options.body: A particle of water is the same particle in ice and in steam. All that changes is how it moves.

options.subtitle: Every model here is 15 billion times life size

options.title: Water: 104.5°
options.body: Two lone pairs on the oxygen, the pale lobes, push the hydrogens closer together than a tetrahedron’s 109.5°. The O–H bond is 0.096 nm.

options.title: Methane: 109.5°
options.body: Four bonds and no lone pairs spread as far apart as they can in 3D. Flat on paper it looks like 90°. It is not.

options.title: Ammonia: 107°
options.body: Three bonds and one lone pair, so a pyramid. Compare the angle with methane (no lone pairs) and water (two).

options.title: Carbon dioxide: 180°
options.body: Two double bonds and nothing on the carbon to bend them, so a straight line. Same formula shape as water, completely different molecule.

options.title: Ethanol
options.body: Water with one hydrogen swapped for a carbon chain. That –OH is why it mixes with water, and why it melts and boils so differently from methane.

options.title: Benzene
options.body: Six carbons in a flat ring, and all six bonds are the same length: 0.139 nm, between a single and a double bond. The thin inner sticks show that.

options.title: Caffeine
options.body: Twenty-four atoms, from PubChem’s computed shape. Red double bonds, blue nitrogens. Mostly flat, because of the two joined rings.

options.title: There is no salt molecule
options.body: Each sodium ion (purple) has six chloride neighbours (green), and each chloride six sodiums, without end. The lines are guides to the pattern, not bonds.

options.title: The packed half
options.body: Here the ions touch at their real sizes: Na+ 102 pm, Cl- 181 pm. This model is 7.6 billion times life size, and has 216 ions. A 1 mm grain has about 4.5 x 10^19.

options.title: Why salt melts at 1074 K
options.body: Pulling a crystal apart means fighting every neighbour’s charge at once. Water molecules only hold on to each other weakly. Now try salt’s numbers on the thermostat.

options.title: Make a water molecule
steps: A red sphere for the oxygen, about 2 ft across.
Two small white spheres for the hydrogens.
Stretch two white cylinders for the bonds.
Use Rotate/Move Shape to open them to 104.5 degrees. Rotation snaps to 15, so get as close as you can.
Connect them all, then Render Model.
options.tip: Walk to the real one in the Molecule Garden and compare.
